Acids donate protons, bases accept them, and pH expresses hydronium concentration logarithmically.

In the Brønsted–Lowry model, an acid donates H⁺ and a base accepts H⁺. Buffers use a weak acid/base conjugate pair to consume small additions of acid or base.

theory:
Potassium dichromate and potassium permanganate are strongly coloured transition-metal oxidants whose products depend on reaction conditions.

Acidified dichromate, Cr2O7^2-, is reduced from Cr(VI) to green Cr3+; acidified permanganate, MnO4-, is reduced from Mn(VII) to nearly colourless Mn2+. In neutral or weakly alkaline medium permanganate commonly forms brown MnO2. Preparation, colour changes and balanced ionic equations are central board requirements.

theory:
Metal carbonyl bonding is synergic: carbon monoxide donates a lone pair to the metal while the metal back-donates d-electron density into CO antibonding orbitals.

Sigma donation forms M<-CO bonding and pi back-bonding strengthens M-C while weakening C-O. Greater back-donation lowers the C-O stretching frequency. Electron counting explains stable examples such as Ni(CO)4 and Fe(CO)5, while bridging and terminal carbonyls differ structurally and spectroscopically.

theory:
Acidity and basicity explains proton transfer and the resulting composition of aqueous solutions, including indicator changes and quantitative pH behavior. Learning goal: explain Acidity and basicity inside Principles of Organic Chemistry, predict one observable result, and justify the answer with evidence. Evaluate evidence quality, uncertainty, model limits and research-level applications.

In the Brønsted–Lowry model, an acid donates H⁺ and a base accepts H⁺. In water these transfers establish equilibria, so strength and concentration are different ideas. pH is logarithmic: a change of one pH unit corresponds to a tenfold change in hydronium concentration. Buffers use a weak acid/base conjugate pair to consume small additions of acid or base.
